Participants with a life expectancy of less than three years, or those with conditions or characteristics that would interfere with study participation and adherence (such as alcoholism, drug dependency, mental illness, or dementia), were excluded. Additionally, individuals actively participating in another randomized clinical trial were not eligible. 2. Participants in the intervention group received either 5 mg of conjugated equine estrogens (CEE) combined with medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) or a matched placebo. In the observational study (OS) group, there were no restrictions on hormone use. 3. Lactation history was assessed using the WHI Reproductive History Questionnaire. It was categorized based on the number of children breastfed (1–2, 3–5, and more than 5), the age at first and last breastfeeding (<20 years, 20–24 years, 25–29 years, 30–34 years, and ≥35 years), and the cumulative lifetime duration of lactation (1–3 months, 4–12 months, 13–23 months, and ≥24 months). Women who reported breastfeeding for less than one month were classified as having no breastfeeding history. 4. Risk of bias was evaluated across several domains, including confounding, participant selection, exposure classification, deviations from intended exposures, incomplete outcome data (attrition bias), outcome measurement, selective reporting, and other biases. In all these domains, the risk of bias was judged to be unclear. 5. The Norwegian Mother and Child Study (MoBa) was a prospective birth cohort study conducted between 1999 and 2008, recruiting expecting mothers from across Norway. Only singleton births with completed questionnaires at 6 and 18 months of age were included. Children with missing data for any study variables were excluded from the analysis. 6. From 6 to 18 months of age, mothers reported breastfeeding status at four intervals: 6–8 months, 9–11 months, 12–14 months, and 15–18 months. The outcomes assessed included relative risks for infections such as acute gastroenteritis, acute otitis media, respiratory tract infections, and all infections combined. 7. The Nurses’ Health Study (NHS), initiated in 1976, enrolled 121,700 women aged 30–55 years from 11 U.S. states. Participants completed detailed baseline questionnaires on medical diagnoses, lifestyle, reproductive history, and other variables. Follow-up questionnaires were administered biennially to update medical and health-related information. 8. In 1986, lactation history was assessed as a categorical variable based on the total duration of breastfeeding across all pregnancies. Lifetime lactation history was stratified into six groups: none, >0–3 months, >3–6 months, >6–11 months, >11–23 months, and >23 months. Outcomes included the incidence of nonfatal myocardial infarction, coronary heart disease mortality, and other health conditions. 9. The Nurses’ Health Study II (NHS II), launched in 1989, enrolled 116,608 women aged 25–42 years, primarily Caucasian registered nurses. The study was restricted to women who reported at least one pregnancy by 1997, when detailed breastfeeding data were collected. Exclusion criteria included nulliparity, missing parity data, postmenopausal status, prevalent breast cancer, and other malignancies. 10. In 1997, participants completed a detailed questionnaire on breastfeeding and lactation suppression for their first four children. Women with more than four children reported the total months of breastfeeding across all additional pregnancies. Breastfeeding duration was categorized, and lifetime contributions from all pregnancies were summed. 11. Project Viva recruited women at their first prenatal visit in Eastern Massachusetts. Eligibility criteria included fluency in English, gestational age <22 weeks, and singleton pregnancy. Breastfeeding intention and initiation were assessed at 28 weeks’ gestation and shortly after delivery. Follow-up visits at 6 months and 12 months postpartum collected data on breastfeeding duration and the introduction of supplemental foods. 12. The Polish-Norwegian Study (PONS) project collected cross-sectional data on women aged 37–66 years from southeastern Poland. Breastfeeding history was categorized based on total lifetime duration (never, 1–6 months, 7–12 months, 13–18 months, and >18 months). Outcomes included metabolic syndrome, abdominal obesity, elevated glucose, high blood pressure, and increased triglycerides. 13. The Fukuoka Child Health Study (FCHS) in Japan examined the association between breastfeeding and child health outcomes. Breastfeeding duration was classified into four categories (<6 months, 6–11 months, 12–17 months, and ≥18 months). Data were collected via structured self-administered questionnaires. 14. A cross-sectional nutritional surveillance survey in Hubei Province, China, included children aged 12–47 months who were initially breastfed for more than 10 days. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into four age groups (<12 months, 12–17 months, 18–23 months, and ≥24 months). Socioeconomic and medical information was also collected. 15. Project Viva also assessed infant feeding practices through mailed questionnaires completed by mothers one year postpartum. Data included breastfeeding duration, timing of weaning, and the introduction of supplemental foods. Outcomes included infant growth metrics and health indicators. 16. A prospective cohort study in East Boston and suburban Holliston followed children from birth to 7 years of age. Physicians collected demographic and health-related data at each pediatric visit, regardless of the visit’s primary purpose.
